papers.canonical_title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. We introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool paradigm, which treats external multimodal large language models as callable visual utilities, and instantiate it in VHarness with five atomic actions: transcribe, grep, inspect, align, and diff. The framework supports iterative Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation, improving visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for multimodal agents and enabling text-only coding agents to perform visually grounded tasks.

source_records.observation: Collected in complete observed cs.CV new listing.
Official title, authors, abstract, v1 timestamp and versioned PDF link.

papers.screening_reason: A coding agent autonomously invokes visual tools, executes code that creates SVG and Blender artifacts, renders them, and uses visual feedback to revise the artifact.

screening_evidence.evidence: The coding agent chooses among code writing/editing and five external visual utilities; rendered artifacts are used for iterative refinement.
Tasks include Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D, with agents producing pure SVG or Blender Python scripts and rendering them for comparison.

task.evidence: The principal task is iterative visual coding for SVG and procedural 3D modeling, with HTML as an additional structured visual artifact.

input_form.evidence: Image-to-SVG takes raster target images; Image-to-3D takes four views of a 3D object.

output.evidence: The agent outputs SVG code, Blender Python code, and rendered artifacts/GLB meshes.

model_type.evidence: The agent can be multimodal or text-only while external visual utilities are powered by an MLLM; the deployed system is therefore hybrid.
model_type.reasoning: The decision-maker and callable visual MLLM jointly comprise the agentic system.

model_training.evidence: Experiments use named pretrained coding agents and Gemini-3.8-Flash as the utility model; no task-specific training of the agentic controller is reported.
model_training.reasoning: Use of pretrained models without reported task fine-tuning supports Off-the-Shelf for the analyzed deployment.

planning.evidence: The agent autonomously chooses tools and iterations rather than following a fixed workflow.
planning.reasoning: Dynamic tool and revision decisions support PO-3 rather than a fixed plan.

workflow.evidence: Code generation, rendering, visual inspection, diagnosis and revision form a loop with alternative callable actions.
workflow.reasoning: The tool-mediated loop has non-linear action choices and feedback dependencies, so Graph-Structured is more accurate than merely Sequential.

update_strategy.evidence: The agent makes targeted code updates after diff/inspect feedback and can replan by choosing subsequent utilities and revisions.

verifier.evidence: External MLLM utilities inspect and compare rendered artifacts; align returns Boolean assertions and diff diagnoses discrepancies.

feedback_assessment.evidence: align returns a Boolean match judgment while diff returns ranked discrepancy diagnoses.

feedback_observation.evidence: Utilities observe rendered pixels and localized visual/structural discrepancies.

memory_time.evidence: The formulation conditions later code updates on prior thoughts, code updates, rendered images and utility feedback within one execution.
memory_time.reasoning: No cross-run persistence is described; retained trajectory context is working execution memory.

memory_reach.evidence: The coding agent uses feedback from its own current artifact trajectory.
memory_reach.reasoning: No global multi-agent memory is reported; memory is local to the execution.

action_type.evidence: The agent writes/edits HTML, SVG and Blender Python and invokes MCP visual tools.

graphics_software.evidence: VHarness adds an MCP adapter exposing graphics perception and verification utilities to existing coding agents and renderers.
graphics_software.reasoning: The underlying renderers are general-purpose; the agent-facing VHarness adapter makes the interface Agent-Adapted.

tools.evidence: Five callable visual utilities perform structure extraction, localization, inspection, assertion checking and image comparison.

resources.evidence: Image-to-HTML uses provided visual assets; task skills and exact tool prompts supply rules/documentation.

representation.evidence: The workflow uses HTML/SVG/Blender code, 3D geometry/GLB, layouts and rendered pixels.

papers.contribution: Introduces Vision-as-a-Tool and VHarness, a general MCP-based visual utility interface that lets coding agents invoke transcribe, grep, inspect, align and diff during closed-loop visual artifact generation and refinement.
papers.limitations: The experiments focus on static single-page, standalone vector, and individual-object 3D reconstruction tasks; the paper explicitly leaves interactive applications and temporal 3D scenes for future work, and the system substantially increases token/tool usage.
papers.analysis_target: Task-time VHarness controller and its visual feedback loop for agentic SVG and procedural 3D artifact generation; the external MLLM utilities are an enabling subsystem within that deployed loop.

agent_graphics_relation.controller: The coding agent Pθ, augmented by VHarness callable visual utilities Uϕ
agent_graphics_relation.action_or_decision: Selects visual tools, writes/edits code, renders, diagnoses discrepancies and decides subsequent revisions
agent_graphics_relation.graphics_target: Rendered HTML/SVG images and Blender-generated 3D geometry/GLB artifacts
agent_graphics_relation.evidence: The paper states that the agent autonomously invokes visual utilities during execution and evaluates Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D generation with iterative rendered-artifact refinement.

papers.canonical_title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
papers.abstract: SCENEAGENT is a multi-agent framework for portable 3D game-scene construction. A canonical SceneContext stores evolving world state, backend adapters isolate engine-specific realization, fresh Builder sessions coordinate through structured handoffs, and human-approved traces are distilled into reusable Layout and Content skills. GameSceneBench evaluates 69 indoor and outdoor prompts across engines and baselines.
papers.screening_reason: Planner and Builder agents directly create and edit a canonical 3D scene state through construction tools, geometry checks and backend adapters.

screening_evidence.evidence: Orchestrator, Planner and fresh Builder sessions modify shared SceneContext through asset, placement, procedural layout, query and targeted-editing tools.
The supplementary interface lists scene-changing construction tools, rollback/edit operations and collision verification.

task.evidence: The system constructs complete 3D game environments and scene layouts.

input_form.evidence: The method accepts text prompts or reference images.

output.evidence: It produces an executable game scene via canonical structured SceneContext and backend export payloads.

model_type.evidence: DeepSeek-V4-Flash is used for Orchestrator, Planner and Builder decisions; cross-model experiments use other LLMs.

model_training.evidence: The deployed construction agents use named language-model backbones; no task-specific controller fine-tuning is reported.
model_training.reasoning: The method evaluates prompting/orchestration over pretrained LLMs rather than reporting supervised or RL adaptation of the decision-maker.

planning.evidence: An Orchestrator and Planner create an ordered queue of semantic subtasks, while Builders execute them and refinement may revise the scene.
planning.reasoning: The plan is partly explicit and partly model-generated, supporting hybrid PO-2.

workflow.evidence: Subtasks, fresh Builder sessions, shared state queries, reports, validation and refinement have non-linear dependencies.
workflow.reasoning: The multi-agent handoff and validation structure is graph-like rather than a single fixed path.

update_strategy.evidence: Builders perform targeted editing and rollback; Orchestrator can revise the plan and invoke bounded refinement.

verifier.evidence: Automatic geometry checks diagnose violations; a human quality gate approves or rejects experience updates.

feedback_assessment.evidence: Geometry checks produce violation diagnoses; human review makes approve/reject decisions.

feedback_observation.evidence: SceneContext exposes actor transforms, bounding boxes, occupancy, provenance and renderings.

memory_time.evidence: SceneContext persists evolving world state across Builder sessions and skill libraries persist approved experience across generations.

memory_reach.evidence: SceneContext is shared across Builder sessions and Layout/Content skills are retrieved by future Orchestrator/Planner/Builder runs.

action_type.evidence: Agents invoke construction tools and provide structured subtask specifications and reports.

graphics_software.evidence: The agent-facing shared tool interface is adapted across backend engines through adapters and capability wrappers.
graphics_software.reasoning: The system adds a normalized agent interface over general game/scene engines, making the software Agent-Adapted.

tools.evidence: Asset retrieval, placement, procedural geometry, scene queries, targeted editing, rollback and collision checks are callable workflow tools.

resources.evidence: Backend asset catalogs, approved Layout/Content traces, construction guides and shared conventions are accessed by the agents.

representation.evidence: Canonical geometry and layouts are stored as actor-centric SceneContext, with backend export code/payloads and reusable skills.

papers.contribution: Provides a portable multi-agent 3D scene-construction protocol separating canonical scene state, task-local reasoning, reusable experience and backend-specific realization.
papers.limitations: Porting still requires backend adapters, compatible assets and capability wrappers; multi-agent coordination adds substantial runtime, human approval limits experience-update scalability, and rendered-view/geometry checks do not establish physical stability, navigability or gameplay success.
papers.analysis_target: Task-time Orchestrator–Planner–Builder subsystem for constructing and refining portable 3D game scenes, with cross-run skill extraction as a secondary experience-update phase.

agent_graphics_relation.controller: SCENEAGENT Orchestrator, Planner and fresh Builder agents
agent_graphics_relation.action_or_decision: Decompose prompts, retrieve skills, select assets, place/edit actors, query SceneContext, validate geometry and refine/export the scene
agent_graphics_relation.graphics_target: Canonical 3D SceneContext and exported game-engine scene
agent_graphics_relation.evidence: The paper explicitly describes agents modifying SceneContext through construction tools and geometry gates, then exporting through backend adapters.

papers.canonical_title: RecurIR: Learning When and How to Revise Restoration Policies via Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: RecurIR is a recursive self-improvement framework for agent-based image restoration. Policy-hypothesis discovery learns condition-dependent relationships between degradation states and restoration plans; rule-falsification-driven task evolution generates targeted degradation variations; change-conditioned policy revision adjusts tool selection, order, operation strength and processing regions. Independent transfer and retention tests accept or reject updates.

source_records.observation: Full 17-page PDF including supplementary material read.

papers.screening_reason: The restoration agent selects and revises image-processing actions that directly modify image artifacts, using visual/quality feedback and programmatic acceptance tests.

screening_evidence.evidence: The agent selects restoration tools and revises plans in tool choice, order, strength and processing regions as degradation conditions change.
Restored images are evaluated with quality measures, rollback/success criteria and transfer-retention tests controlling policy updates.

task.evidence: The principal task is adaptive restoration of degraded images.

input_form.evidence: The agent receives a degraded image and generic restoration instruction, while degradation state is estimated from image observations.

output.evidence: The workflow outputs restored images and revised restoration plans.

model_type.evidence: The system combines learned policy modules, a restoration planner and a library of specialized restoration networks/tools.
model_type.reasoning: The controller is a learned policy system operating through heterogeneous restoration models, so Hybrid best describes the decision subsystem.

model_training.evidence: PDM and CPRM are optimized with explicit classification/regression objectives; supplementary details describe agent training while restoration tools remain frozen.

planning.evidence: The agent selects tool sequences and parameters, then conditionally revises them based on degradation changes.
planning.reasoning: The restoration plan is partly learned and partly constrained by the available tool library, supporting hybrid PO-2.

workflow.evidence: Tool execution follows a selected restoration plan, with regional operations and subsequent revisions in an ordered pipeline.

update_strategy.evidence: The controller edits tool selection/order/strength/regions, replans under changed conditions, and selects candidate updates through transfer-retention validation.

verifier.evidence: Quality metrics, severe-artifact detection, transfer validation and retention validation accept or reject candidate policy updates.

feedback_assessment.evidence: PSNR/SSIM and related quality scores provide graded feedback; falsification uses diagnosis of rule contradictions; update acceptance is binary under transfer-retention thresholds.

feedback_observation.evidence: The system observes degraded/restored pixels, degradation severity and spatial distribution, and image-quality/artifact states.

memory_time.evidence: Verified hypotheses, applicability regions and revision evidence are retained and reused across recursive improvement rounds.

memory_reach.evidence: The accumulated hypotheses and revisions are used by the restoration policy and task-generation components; no cross-system shared memory is reported.
memory_reach.reasoning: The memory is persistent for the local agent/policy rather than described as globally shared across independent agents.

action_type.evidence: The agent invokes specialized restoration tools and emits structured plans containing tools, order, parameters and regions.

graphics_software.evidence: The agent is built around a shared restoration-tool library and an agent-facing coordination layer rather than direct native GUI authoring.
graphics_software.reasoning: The tool adapter and policy interface are tailored to agentic restoration, so Agent-Adapted is appropriate.

tools.evidence: The shared library contains deraining, desnowing, dehazing, deblurring, denoising and all-in-one restoration tools; perception and quality checks guide use.

resources.evidence: The agent uses a shared pretrained restoration-tool library, degradation rules and accumulated verified hypotheses/evidence.

representation.evidence: The workflow operates on image pixels and stores learned condition-dependent hypotheses and revision operators.

papers.contribution: Introduces a recursive self-improvement loop that discovers condition-dependent restoration rules, actively falsifies them with targeted degradation changes, and learns verified revisions to tool selection, order, strength and regions.
papers.limitations: The framework relies on controllable degradation generation, reference-based training supervision and a fixed restoration-tool library; its quality gains and recursive updates are evaluated primarily through image-restoration benchmarks and may not establish general-purpose visual editing beyond restoration.
papers.analysis_target: Training/data-generation phase of the RecurIR restoration-policy subsystem, with task-time image restoration as its deployed graphics action; the paper's principal novelty is learning when and how to revise the controller's tool-use rules.

agent_graphics_relation.controller: RecurIR restoration agent and its PDM/RTEM/CPRM policy modules
agent_graphics_relation.action_or_decision: Selects restoration tools and sequences, changes operation strength and processing regions, and accepts or rejects revised policies
agent_graphics_relation.graphics_target: Degraded image pixels and restored image artifacts
agent_graphics_relation.evidence: The paper explicitly defines restoration plans over image observations, applies them through specialized tools, and uses image-quality and artifact feedback to revise those plans.

papers.canonical_title: TelePhysica: Agentic Reconstruction of Physically Interactive Scenes
papers.abstract: TelePhysica reconstructs an executable, physically interactive world from a single photograph. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models, then uses pixel-aligned silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational equilibrium verification before compiling rigid, articulated, cloth and volumetric dynamics. Simulated trajectories condition video diffusion for stateful and counterfactual interactions.

events.evidence: PDF front matter and official arXiv metadata; target-local time 2026-11-13T06:02:43-06:00.

papers.screening_reason: A vision-language coding agent directly creates and revises 3D graphics and physical scene state, with rendered and solver feedback controlling subsequent scene edits.

screening_evidence.evidence: The reconstruction agent synthesizes procedural visual meshes and physical models, then revises them using silhouette and equilibrium diagnostics.
The evaluated system constructs scenes, runs physical interventions and feeds verified trajectories to video generation.

task.evidence: The principal purpose is reconstructing and simulating physically interactive 3D scenes, including rigid, articulated and deformable regimes.

input_form.evidence: The agent receives a single photograph and a scene description.

output.evidence: The system emits executable scene programs/physical models, verified 3D worlds and rendered trajectory-conditioned videos.

model_type.evidence: A vision-language coding agent controls code generation and verification while physics solvers and video diffusion provide downstream execution/rendering.
model_type.reasoning: The deployed graphics agent combines a VLM controller with procedural graphics, physics and video components, so Hybrid is appropriate.

model_training.evidence: The paper uses pretrained coding/video models and reports no task-specific training of the reconstruction controller.
model_training.reasoning: The decision-maker is used as a pretrained model with prompting/tool interaction; no controller fine-tuning is reported.

planning.evidence: The agent iteratively proposes scripts, renders, critiques, repairs and re-verifies candidate worlds.
planning.reasoning: The next actions are selected at inference time rather than fixed in a complete hard-coded plan, supporting PO-3.

workflow.evidence: Stage-1 visual reconstruction precedes Stage-2 equilibrium verification, followed by physics rollout and video conditioning.

update_strategy.evidence: The agent locally repairs camera, geometry, poses, roles and colliders; it replans after structured failures and selects only verified scene submissions.

verifier.evidence: Silhouette/edge diagnostics, a deterministic physics solver and equilibrium gates judge candidate worlds; the environment exposes solver health and drift.

feedback_assessment.evidence: Mask/edge metrics provide scores, diagnostic overlays and contact/drift traces provide diagnoses, and threshold gates accept or reject candidates.

feedback_observation.evidence: The loop observes rendered pixels and masks, structural geometry/contact state, and solver runtime/health and drift traces.

memory_time.evidence: The agent and solver retain scene programs, current state, contact state and checkpoints during reconstruction and rollout.

memory_reach.evidence: State and diagnostics are available to the current reconstruction/rollout controller; no cross-run or multi-agent shared memory is described.
memory_reach.reasoning: The retained state is local to the current execution and checkpointed world.

action_type.evidence: The VLM writes procedural 3D scripts/declarative physical models and invokes rendering, physics and verification execution.

graphics_software.evidence: The agent-facing interface combines headless rendering, procedural scene compilation and solver adapters.
graphics_software.reasoning: These adapters expose general graphics and physics engines through a dedicated agent workflow, making the software Agent-Adapted.

tools.evidence: Rendering/mask analysis, procedural mesh compilation, rigid and finite-element physics solvers, checkpoint/replay and video conditioning are callable capabilities in the workflow.

resources.evidence: The system accesses asset/material priors, declarative physical rules, procedural schemas and pretrained video/renderer components.

representation.evidence: The workflow uses procedural code, explicit meshes/geometry, dynamic mechanical state, simulation trajectories and rendered pixels.

papers.contribution: Introduces a closed-loop agentic reconstruction framework that converts a single photograph into a mechanically verified, executable multi-regime physical world and uses its simulated trajectories to ground video synthesis.
papers.limitations: Material parameters are assigned from priors rather than identified online from multi-step visual interaction feedback; the method depends on a fixed solver/model stack and expensive rendering/physics/video components, and its verification is limited to the reported scene regimes and tests.
papers.analysis_target: Task-time reconstruction agent and its visual/physical verification loop; trajectory-conditioned video synthesis is a downstream rendering phase, not mixed into the controller's primary feedback taxonomy.

agent_graphics_relation.action_or_decision: Writes procedural meshes and physical models, renders candidates, interprets silhouette/contact/drift diagnostics and revises scene code before executing interventions
agent_graphics_relation.graphics_target: Executable 3D visual meshes, colliders, finite-element models and their rendered physical rollouts
agent_graphics_relation.evidence: The paper explicitly describes an agent that synthesizes and edits scene programs inside a two-stage pixel and gravitational-equilibrium verification loop.

papers.canonical_title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
papers.abstract: ImpedanceMimic is a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping and position setpoints to imitate human motion while reproducing measured contact forces. It controls subject-specific MuJoCo biomechanical models, transfers to unseen humans and a simulated humanoid robot, and learns an interpretable impedance representation of motor state.

source_records.observation: Full 39-page PDF read; pages 1-39 delivered across two receipts.

papers.screening_reason: The paper provides an RL controller for simulated articulated human and humanoid bodies, but its principal target is biomechanical force recovery rather than graphics authoring or a graphics-agent task. It is retained as borderline because the controller acts on an executable dynamic character environment and the paper explicitly connects the setting to physics-based character animation.

screening_evidence.evidence: The controller changes joint impedance in MuJoCo worlds and produces simulated motion/contact forces, while the stated objective is biomechanical force-accurate imitation.
Experiments evaluate human and humanoid simulation control, not visual asset authoring, scene construction or rendered-media generation.

task.evidence: The principal task is physics-based motion imitation and contact-force recovery in articulated body simulation; animation is a secondary graphics interpretation.

input_form.evidence: Reference motion trajectories and simulated 3D body state are inputs; the method uses motion data rather than a user graphics-authoring request.

output.evidence: The controller outputs joint impedance/setpoint actions and produces simulated dynamic states and character motion.

model_type.evidence: The decision policy is an MLP actor in an RL controller; no LLM or VLM is used.
model_type.reasoning: The taxonomy has no dedicated RL-policy label, and the model is not an LLM/VLM/hybrid graphics agent, so Not Applicable is used for this graphics-agent analysis.

model_training.evidence: The actor and critic are trained with PPO for 2 billion simulation steps using motion and force rewards.

planning.evidence: The policy emits an action at each control step; no explicit multi-step task plan is represented.
planning.reasoning: A fixed per-step control loop without a separate plan representation is PO-1.

workflow.evidence: Reference observations, policy action, PD simulation and reward computation repeat in one ordered control loop.

update_strategy.evidence: The policy continuously changes joint gains and position offsets in response to current simulated state.
update_strategy.reasoning: The update is a local control action on the current dynamic state, not artifact regeneration or global replanning.

verifier.evidence: MuJoCo physics executes the controller and computes contact forces; reward and evaluation metrics quantify tracking and force fidelity.

feedback_assessment.evidence: Rewards and evaluation metrics provide continuous scores, while termination and numerical-invalid-state checks provide diagnostic/binary outcomes.

feedback_observation.evidence: The actor observes proprioception, contact state, lookahead motion/force estimates and foot state; simulator runtime and termination are also used.

memory_time.evidence: The lagged gain state and current simulated state persist within an episode/control rollout, with reset at episode initialization.

memory_reach.evidence: State is available to the single actor/environment loop; no shared or cross-run agent memory is described.
memory_reach.reasoning: The controller's state is local to one control process.

action_type.evidence: The policy emits structured numerical impedance parameters and setpoints that are passed to the PD controller/simulator.

graphics_software.evidence: The method directly uses MuJoCo Warp and a general-purpose articulated-body simulator without a graphics-specific agent adapter.

tools.evidence: MuJoCo Warp, PD control and physical contact computation are callable execution/solver components; kinematic-to-GRF estimation provides observation support.

resources.evidence: The system uses motion/force trajectories from nine datasets, biomechanical model rules and simulator configurations.

representation.evidence: The workflow represents articulated geometry, joint/dynamic state, contact forces and learned impedance trajectories.

papers.contribution: Introduces an RL controller that learns state-dependent joint impedance for force-accurate physics-based motion imitation and transfers across human and robot embodiments.
papers.limitations: The principal contribution is biomechanics and simulated control rather than graphics authoring; the method depends on motion/force supervision, a fixed biomechanical model and MuJoCo simulation, and uses future reference lookahead in its estimator/observations.
papers.analysis_target: Task-time RL control of an articulated simulated body; retained as borderline because the action relation is demonstrated in a dynamic graphics-adjacent simulation, but the paper does not establish an agentic graphics-authoring objective.

agent_graphics_relation.action_or_decision: Modulates per-joint stiffness, damping and position setpoints at each simulation step
agent_graphics_relation.graphics_target: Simulated articulated human bodies and a Unitree G1 humanoid dynamic state
agent_graphics_relation.evidence: The policy directly controls articulated simulated bodies and produces motion/contact trajectories, but the paper's target is biomechanical force recovery rather than graphics artifact authoring; the graphics-scope connection is therefore incomplete.
